newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU forecasts show Germany missing EMU target - paper.
newsitem.headline: EU forecasts show Germany missing EMU target - paper.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to show that Germany will be unable to bring its 1997 budget deficit down to three percent of Gross Domestic Product, a Portuguese newspaper reported on Thursday.

According to the report, published in El Publico, Germany's 1997 budget deficit will be 3.2 percent of GDP, just above the three percent target set in the Maastricht treaty to qualify for economic and monetary union.

Speculation that Bonn would have a tough time adhering strictly to the deficit target has been rampant in recent weeks, with sluggish growth and high unemployment contributing to an increasingly uncertain budget outlook.

Quoted in a magazine article on Thursday, Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said: "It is becoming increasingly evident that Germany will find it extraordinarily difficult to meet the budget and debt criteria."
He also said that any delay to the planned January 1, 1999 start date for monetary union could not be ruled out.

In contrast to such pessimism, German finance minister Theo Waigel said on Thursday recent economic data would not force Bonn to abandon its budget forecasts. But should there be a need for additional measures, Waigel said Germany would be ready to act.
His views were echoed by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl who together with French president Jacques Chirac reaffirmed their expectations for a timely launch of the common currency.

The Portuguese newspaper report, which also showed Italy's 1997 deficit at 3.8 percent of total output, was played down by Commission officials, who noted that the actual forecasts would not be ready until April 23.
"We have nothing to do with the table. Work on the forecast is still continuing," a spokesman said.
When asked whether the table was wrong, the spokesman said: "We never make any comment on this sort of press speculation."

For France and Spain, the report showed both countries meeting the Maastricht target. Overall, 12 out 15 countries were at or below the three percent deficit target, with only Germany, Greece and Italy not qualifying.
A representative from the newspaper told Reuters that the figures had been obtained from the Commission.
In the past, the Commission has been known to revise its economic estimates just days before an official release date, raising the possiblity that further revisions might be made.

An Italian Treasury source said Italy's recently introduced mini-budget would bring this year's deficit down to 3.0 percent of GDP. The source added that the reported 3.8 percent figure referred to state accounts before the mini-budget was presented.

While meeting the deficit target has attracted the most attention among the numerous criteria countries must fulfil in order to join EMU, officials caution there will also be a determination of whether budget consolidation is sustainable.
EU monetary commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy recently said such an assessment will include a look at 1998 budget estimates.
Following are the reported deficit estimates by the Commission due on April 23:
Spring 1997
Belgium 2.8 pct
Denmark 0.3
Germany 3.2
Greece 4.9
Spain 3.0
France 3.0
Ireland 0.8
Italy 3.8
Luxembourg 1.1
Netherlands 2.2
Austria 3.0
Portugal 3.0
Finland 1.9
Sweden 2.9
Britain 3.0
